subject: korean
title: Which sign leads to the parking lot?
goal: Read three short road signs, combine the words with the arrow and symbol described, and judge which one really leads a visitor to park; defend the judgement against a friend's half-reading.
thinking: Combining word, symbol and arrow as evidence
Not stopping at one familiar word (주차장)
Answering a friend with evidence from the sign
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what 주차장 or 출구 means. Here three signs all contain familiar words, and you must decide which one is meant for a driver who wants to park, using every part of each sign.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul syllables aloud
Knows that an arrow on a sign shows the way to go
material:
A visitor drives up to a school and wants to leave the car for one hour. Three signs are in view (no pictures, so they are described in words).

Sign A: white letters '주차 금지' on a red board. A red circle with a diagonal line crosses a small drawing of a car. It is fixed to the school fence.
Sign B: blue board, white letters '방문자 주차장' and an arrow pointing to the right. It stands at the side of the road.
Sign C: green board, white letters '주차장 출구' and an arrow pointing back toward the road. It hangs over a narrow lane where cars are driving out.

Words: 주차(장) = parking (lot); 방문자 = visitor; 입구 = entrance; 출구 = exit.

steps.prompt: Which sign should the visitor follow in order to park?
hints: List what each sign says in words, and what its symbol or arrow adds.
Ask of each sign: does it send a car in, out, or nowhere?

options.reveals: 주차장 is in this sign, but it is only one word of two. Check what the second word and the arrow say about the direction cars take.
This sign has 주차 too. Look at the red circle with the slash: what does that kind of symbol usually tell you?
You combined the visitor word, the parking word and the arrow. That is how a sign is read as a whole.

options.text: Sign B or Sign C; both say 주차장 and have an arrow
options.reveals: Both do say 주차장 and have an arrow, but check what the other word of Sign C and the direction of its arrow say.

steps.explain: Sign B is for visitors, names a parking lot and gives a direction. Sign A has the same first word but carries a prohibition symbol. Sign C names a parking lot too, but 출구 means exit, so it marks where cars leave.

steps.prompt: A friend says: 'Sign C has 주차장 in it, so let's drive in through there.' Answer your friend in one or two English sentences, using what the sign actually says.
hints: Which word of Sign C is different from Sign B's?
Where do cars go on a lane that has an exit sign?

checks.label: connects it to leaving, or to needing the entrance

selfAssess: Did I use the word of the sign as evidence, not just my opinion?
Did I say what the sign is for (leaving) and what we need instead?
Would my friend know where to look next?

modelAnswers.text: Sign C says 출구, which means exit. Cars drive out there, so we should look for an entrance, like the arrow on Sign B.
modelAnswers.note: Names the key word and the missing entrance.

modelAnswers.text: 주차장 is only half of it. The other word, 출구, tells us cars are leaving there, so we would be driving the wrong way.
modelAnswers.note: Explains the risk with the direction.

badAnswers.text: Sign A is better because it has a red board.
badAnswers.why: Ignores the friend's claim and the words of Sign C.

badAnswers.text: I think it is fine, 주차장 means parking.
badAnswers.why: Repeats half of the sign and skips 출구.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reply gives the right evidence politely and clearly; alternative wordings with the same evidence are fine.

rubric.criterion: Uses all parts of the sign
rubric.full: Uses word, symbol and arrow of at least two signs
rubric.partial: Uses the word of one sign only

rubric.full: Names 출구/exit and what it implies
rubric.partial: Says the friend is wrong without the word

alternatives: A learner may also argue that Sign A is the worst choice, which is true, but the question is which sign to follow.
Saying that Sign C may be a second lot with its own entrance is a thoughtful extra, not a mistake.
hardCases: Some real car parks use one sign for both directions; the arrow and 출구/입구 decide, so a learner who has not met 출구 cannot be expected to guess it.

cautions.language: 출구 and 입구 are glossed in the material because K1 learners may not know them; 금지 is deliberately not glossed and must be inferred from the symbol. The arrow is written as 'arrow pointing to the right' in the description.
cautions.culture: Korean road and parking signs follow common international symbols (red circle with slash), and visitor lots are common at schools.
cautions.accessibility: No image is needed: every sign is described in words. A screen reader may read the arrow symbol in Sign B as 'rightwards arrow'; the material also states it in words.

auto: The choice of sign against the key
Presence of 출구/exit and leaving/entrance words in the reply
human: Quality and politeness of the reply to the friend

subject: korean
topic: What a sign does and does not say
title: If it rains, is the picnic on?
goal: Compare a note taken in English with the original Korean notice, find the line that says more than the notice, and write the Korean rule yourself.
thinking: Checking a summary line by line against the source
Noticing a condition ('if') turned into a fact
Rewriting the condition in Korean
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what 소풍 or 도시락 means. Here the words are easy; the thinking is whether a classmate's note keeps the condition of the original sentence or turns it into something it never said.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul and short polite sentences
Has met the ending -(으)면 and the idea of 'if' in simple sentences
material:
A teacher stuck a notice on the classroom door:

내일은 소풍 가요.
9시까지 학교에 오세요.
도시락을 가져오세요.
비가 오면 소풍을 안 가요.

Words: 소풍 = outing/picnic; 도시락 = lunch box; 비 = rain; 오다 = to come (비가 오다 = it rains); 안 = not.

Joon read it and wrote four notes in English (shown below).

More words (for step 2): 눈 = snow (눈이 오다 = it snows); 공원 = park.

steps.prompt: One of Joon's notes says more than the notice says. Which line?
hints: Compare each note with the notice, one line at a time.
Which note states something as certain that the notice only states as a condition?
lines: We must be at school by 9.
It will rain tomorrow, so there is no picnic.
steps.explain: Line 4 is the problem. The notice says what happens if it rains (비가 오면); it does not say that it will rain. Joon turned a condition into a prediction.

steps.prompt: Another notice, said in English: "If it snows tomorrow, we do not go to the park." Write this rule in Korean (polite -요 speech), using the words above.
hints: Which two parts must be in the sentence: the condition and what happens?
Check that your sentence does not say that it WILL snow.

checks.label: result: no park (공원 ... 안 가요 / 못 / 없어요 / 취소)

selfAssess: Does my sentence contain 'if it snows' and not 'it snows'?
Does it tell the result for the park?
Is my ending polite?

modelAnswers.note: Close to the pattern of the first notice.
Spoken style with the same meaning.

badAnswers.why: States snow as a fact and keeps the park trip.
Drops the condition completely.
Has the condition, but the result is about a lunch box, not about the park.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sentence is natural; other correct wordings such as 공원은 취소돼요 should be accepted.

rubric.full: Picks the line and says it turns a condition into a fact
rubric.none: Picks a line that is accurate

rubric.full: Sentence has 비가 오면 and a result
rubric.partial: Has only the condition or only the result

alternatives: Some learners may also mark line 2 or 3 because they cannot read 9시 or 도시락; the explanation shows these are accurate.
In s2, a sentence such as 눈이 오면 우산을 가져오세요 is correct Korean but does not say what happens to the park trip.
hardCases: Whether 공원에 못 가요 is as good as 안 가요: it implies cannot rather than will not, so it is accepted but flagged for a human.

cautions.language: -(으)면 is the only grammar point and it is a prerequisite, not taught here. The write check accepts 비 오면 (without 가) because many learners drop the particle.
cautions.culture: 소풍 is a common school outing in Korea; a rain rule on the notice is typical.
cautions.accessibility: No picture is needed. The notice is plain text, one sentence per line, so a screen reader reads it line by line.

auto: Which line was chosen
Surface features of the Korean sentence: polite ending, 눈이 오면, a result word with 공원
human: Naturalness and exact meaning of the written sentence

subject: korean
title: Meet tomorrow at 3. Where?
goal: Decide which piece of information a very short message leaves out and write the Korean question that asks for it.
thinking: Listing what the message gives and what it leaves out
Deciding which missing piece is needed to act
Asking one precise question
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read 만나요 or 3시. Here you read the whole message to find which essential piece is missing and ask only for that.
prerequisites: Can read short Hangul messages and numbers with 시
Knows 내일 and 만나요 from class
material:
Your classmate 지우 sends you a text. You use polite -요 speech with each other.

지우: 내일 3시에 만나요!

Words: 내일 = tomorrow; 3시 = 3 o'clock; 만나요 = (we) meet / let's meet.

steps.prompt: You want to go. Which piece of information do you still need before you can actually meet 지우?
hints: List what the message already tells you: day, time, who, ...
What would you need to know to walk to the right place?

options.reveals: You noticed that the message names a time and a day but nowhere to go.
내일 means tomorrow, so the day is already there.
3시 is the time. Read the message once more from the start.
It could be useful, but you can meet without knowing it, so it is not what blocks you.

steps.explain: The message gives the day (내일), the time (3시) and the sender. The place is missing; without it you cannot meet.

steps.prompt: Write your reply to 지우 in Korean (polite -요 speech): say nothing else, just ask for the missing piece.
hints: Which question word asks about a place?
Finish with a polite ending.
selfAssess: Does my question ask for the place, and only that?
Would 지우 know at once how to answer?
Is it polite?

modelAnswers.note: Repeats the time and suggests a plan.

badAnswers.why: Asks for the time, which the message already gives.
Accepts but leaves the place open.

steps.humanReview: Whether the question is natural; 어디예요? alone is acceptable but less clear.

rubric.full: Names the place and says day and time are given
rubric.none: Names a piece already in the message

rubric.full: Polite question about the place
rubric.partial: Question that is unclear or impolite

alternatives: Asking 어디에서 만날까요? with an own suggestion is also fine.
Some learners reasonably want to ask about the weather; it is useful but not needed to meet.
hardCases: If both 지우's school and a park are likely, a learner may feel the place is 'guessable'; the task treats a guess as not sufficient.

cautions.language: 어디 (where) is the key question word; 어디서 is the spoken short form of 어디에서. The check accepts both.
cautions.culture: Short messages without a place are normal among classmates who share a usual meeting spot, which is why this can feel obvious to native speakers.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The chat is one line, so a screen reader reads it unchanged.

auto: The choice of the missing piece
Presence of 어디 and a polite ending in the reply

subject: korean
title: Who is sick? Messages change the answer
goal: Read a chat one message at a time, keep your guess flexible, and revise who is sick when the next message adds a fact; then answer in Korean.
thinking: Distinguishing what a message says from what we guess
Revising an inference when new evidence arrives
Replying to the real situation
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what 아파요 means. Here you decide, message by message, which guesses are still reasonable and notice when an early guess has to be dropped.
prerequisites: Can read short Hangul messages
Knows basic polite -요 sentences
material:
A classmate, 유나, texts you before school. You know nothing else.

Words: 학교 = school; 못 가요 = cannot go; 병원 = hospital; 동생 = younger brother or sister; 아파요 = (is) sick / hurts; 같이 = together.

The messages arrive one at a time.

steps.prompt: Read each new message and choose what you can reasonably think so far.
hints: Separate what the message says from what you are guessing.
After a new message, ask which earlier guess it supports and which it weakens.

stages.ask: What can you reasonably think so far?

options.reveals: The message gives no reason at all. Sick is a possible guess, not something the message says.

options.text: 유나 will be away from school today; the reason is not given.
options.reveals: You kept to what the message says and left the reason open.
Nothing in the message suggests a move; 오늘 (today) points to one day.

stages.after: The message states only that 유나 cannot come today. Anything about the reason is a guess.

stages.ask: What fits the two messages so far? (Choose all that are reasonable.)

options.text: 유나 is on a holiday trip.
options.reveals: 병원 is a hospital, which does not fit a holiday trip.

options.text: 유나 herself is probably the one who is sick.
options.reveals: A natural first guess; keep it as a guess, not as a fact.

options.text: A hospital visit is the reason, but who needs it is not clear yet.
options.reveals: You kept the question about who open; the message does not name a person.

stages.after: The hospital explains why she is absent, but still not who is sick. Both b and c are reasonable here.

options.text: 유나 is sick and her younger sibling goes along.
options.reveals: Check who is the subject of 아파요 in this message.

options.text: 유나 is sick and also her sibling is.
options.reveals: The message names only the sibling as sick.

options.text: 유나's younger sibling is sick and 유나 goes to the hospital together.
options.reveals: You revised your first guess when 동생이 became the subject.

stages.after: 동생이 is the subject of 아파요, so the sibling is sick. 유나 is absent because she goes along (같이 가요). Your first guess needed to be dropped.

steps.reflect: Your first guess about who is sick was reasonable after the second message but wrong after the third. New evidence can change who the subject of a sentence is, so keep guesses open until the message names the person.

steps.prompt: Write a short Korean reply (polite -요 speech) that shows you understood who is sick.
hints: Which person should your reply mention?
Add a short caring phrase if you can.
selfAssess: Does my reply mention the person who is sick?
Does it sound caring and polite?
Did I avoid saying that 유나 is sick?

modelAnswers.note: Asks about the sibling and shows care.

badAnswers.why: Does not say who; sounds as if 유나 is the sick one.
No Korean content about the situation.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reply is natural and caring; a reply that asks about 유나 herself needs a human to judge.

rubric.full: Chooses the reasonable options at each stage
rubric.partial: Right at the last stage only
rubric.none: Treats the first guess as a fact

rubric.full: Mentions 동생 and shows care politely

alternatives: At stage 2 both 'probably 유나' and 'unclear who' are reasonable; neither is wrong.
A learner may reasonably wish both 유나 and her sibling well; that is fine.
hardCases: 동생이 can be read as 'younger sibling' of either gender; the task does not decide the gender.

cautions.language: 동생 does not show gender; 동생이 아파요 puts the sibling as subject with the particle -이. The glossary gives 동생 so that the thinking, not vocabulary, is tested.
cautions.culture: Taking a younger sibling to the doctor, or staying home to help, is a normal reason for absence in Korean families.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The three messages are plain text and are revealed one at a time, so each stage is a short screen.

auto: Each stage choice against the reasonable list
Presence of a polite ending and 동생 in the reply
human: Naturalness and warmth of the reply

subject: korean
title: Same news for a friend and for a teacher
goal: Rewrite a casual text so that it fits a teacher, and say which parts of the text had to change.
thinking: Judging which parts of a text depend on the reader
Keeping the message and changing the form
Writing a polite message that keeps all the facts
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to turn 가 into 가요. Here you decide what changes for a new reader, and you must keep the facts (cannot come, sick) while changing the style.
prerequisites: Can read short Hangul sentences
Knows the polite -요 ending and the word 선생님
Has seen 저 as the polite word for 'I'
material:
You sent your friend this text:

나 내일 학교에 못 가. 아파.

Now you must tell your teacher (선생님) the same thing in a message.

Words: 내일 = tomorrow; 학교 = school; 못 가 = cannot go; 아파 = (I) am sick.

steps.prompt: Which parts of the friend text must change when it is written for 선생님? Choose all that apply.
hints: Read the text one word at a time and ask: would I say it this way to a teacher?
Say the text aloud as if to your teacher, and notice which words feel wrong.

options.reveals: You noticed that the ending carries the level of politeness.
The day stays the same for any listener; the facts do not change.
The place does not change with the listener.
You noticed that even 'I' has a form for speaking to a teacher.

acceptable.reason: The endings are the main change; changing 나 to 저 is a second, finer one.

steps.explain: The facts (tomorrow, cannot go to school, sick) stay. The endings become polite (-요 or -ㅂ니다), and 나 becomes 저 when speaking to a teacher.

steps.prompt: Write the message to 선생님 in Korean. Keep all the facts of the text and make it suit a teacher.
hints: Which facts must still be in your message?
Start by addressing the teacher.

checks.label: says cannot go (못 가 / 안 가)

selfAssess: Did I keep all the facts?
Does every sentence sound polite to a teacher?
Did I address the teacher or say sorry?

modelAnswers.text: 선생님, 내일 학교에 못 가요. 아파요.
선생님, 안녕하세요. 저는 내일 몸이 아파서 학교에 못 갑니다. 죄송합니다.
선생님, 내일 학교에 갈 수 없습니다. 몸이 아픕니다.

badAnswers.text: 나 내일 학교에 못 가. 아파.
badAnswers.why: Unchanged casual text.
Polite, but changes the fact: it says that you go.

badAnswers.text: 선생님, 저 학교에 못 가요. 아파요.
badAnswers.why: Polite, but drops the day (내일).

steps.humanReview: Whether the tone suits a teacher and the wording is natural; 저 is a bonus, not a requirement.

rubric.full: Says endings (and 나) change, facts stay
Polite message that keeps all facts
rubric.partial: Polite but a fact is lost

alternatives: Both -요 and -ㅂ니다 are valid for a message to a teacher; -ㅂ니다 is more formal.
Some learners add the reason with -아서 (몸이 아파서); it is fine.
hardCases: A message to a teacher with only 죄송해요 and no mention of sickness keeps politeness but loses a fact.

cautions.language: The check accepts 못 가/안 가 and different forms of 가다 and 오다 because learners may say 학교에 못 와요 from the teacher's point of view. 저 (humble I) is not glossed and not required.
cautions.culture: Korean students normally use polite speech to teachers and often add 죄송합니다 when reporting an absence.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The chat text is one short line.

auto: The choice of changing parts
Polite ending, cannot-go, sick and address features of the message
human: Tone, naturalness and whether the facts are all kept

subject: korean
topic: Reading Hangul in labels and names
title: A label for the snack table
goal: Judge which draft labels keep a classmate with a peanut allergy safe and write your own Korean label that says what it must say.
thinking: Deciding what a label must say for its reader
Spotting labels that do not say it, or say the opposite
Producing a short label
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read 쿠키 or 땅콩. Here you decide what information a label has to carry for someone with an allergy and write it yourself.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul words
Knows 있어요 / 없어요
material:
Your class has a snack table. You bring cookies that CONTAIN peanuts. One classmate cannot eat peanuts (allergy). You must put a Korean label on the box.

Words: 쿠키 = cookie; 땅콩 = peanut; 있어요 = there is / it has; 없어요 = there is not; 맛있는 = tasty.

steps.prompt: Which draft labels would keep the classmate safe? Choose all that work.
hints: Check each draft: does it mention peanuts at all?
Then check whether it says the cookies have peanuts or not.

options.reveals: Friendly, but it does not warn about peanuts, so the classmate cannot decide.
You saw that naming the peanut in the cookie is a warning.
It names peanuts, but says the opposite of the truth.
You noticed that 있어요 states that the peanuts are present.

steps.explain: A safe label must say that peanuts are in the cookies. Draft a says nothing about peanuts, and draft c says there are none, which is the worst mistake.

steps.prompt: Now write your own label in Korean for the box. It must tell the reader what is in the box and that it contains peanuts.
hints: Write the food and the warning as two short parts.
Check that your label cannot be read as 'no peanuts'.

checks.label: does not say there are no peanuts
says that the box has peanuts or warns about them

selfAssess: Can a classmate with an allergy understand the warning at a glance?
Is the label short and clear?
Could any part be misread as 'no peanuts'?

badAnswers.why: Says the opposite.
No warning.
Says there are no peanuts, which is the opposite of the truth.
Also says there are no peanuts.

steps.humanReview: Whether the label is natural and clear; labels using 땅콩 주의 or similar need a human to confirm they read as a warning.

rubric.full: Picks the two drafts that state the peanuts
Names cookie and peanut, cannot be misread
rubric.none: Says no peanuts or no warning

alternatives: Labels such as 땅콩 주의 or 땅콩 들어 있음 are good; they may use words not taught at K1.
A label in two lines is as good as one in a sentence.
hardCases: A label that only says 땅콩 쿠키 is accepted but a teacher may want a clearer warning.

cautions.language: In the glossary 있어요/없어요 are given so that the check can look for the opposite. The write check does not require a polite ending because labels are often nouns.
cautions.culture: Food-allergy labels are taken seriously in Korean schools; peanuts are one of the common allergens. The scenario names no real student.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The label is short text; a screen reader reads Korean as normal.

auto: The choice of safe drafts
Presence of 쿠키 and 땅콩 and absence of a 'no peanuts' phrase
human: Whether the label is clear, natural and safe

subject: korean
title: When can you walk into the library?
goal: Read a sign with several lines, decide which lines matter on a given day, then find several arrival times that fit all of them.
thinking: Selecting which lines of a sign apply
Finding several solutions under two limits
Explaining why other times fail
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what 오전 or 쉬어요 means. Here you must satisfy the opening times and the break at once and list times that work.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul and numbers with 시
Knows that 오전 is morning and 오후 is afternoon
material:
A sign on a library door (one line per row):

도서관
오전 9시 ~ 오후 6시
낮 12시 ~ 1시 쉬어요
일요일 쉬어요

Words: 오전 = a.m.; 오후 = p.m.; 낮 = midday; 쉬어요 = (it) rests; ~ is read 'to' (from ... to ...). You want to visit on a Wednesday.

steps.prompt: Which lines of the sign matter for a visit on Wednesday? Choose all that apply.
hints: Ask of each line: does it apply on Wednesday?
One line is a name; one is about another day.

options.reveals: This is the name of the place; it does not limit your time.
You saw that this line gives the hours of a normal day.
You saw that the place stops for a while within the day.
This line is about Sunday; your day is Wednesday.

steps.explain: Lines 2 and 3 apply to every normal day. Line 1 is the name and line 4 is only about Sunday.

steps.prompt: Find three different times on Wednesday at which you can arrive and the library is open. Every time is 'h:30'; enter the hour h on a 24-hour clock (1 p.m. = 13).
hints: Write the opening and closing hours as 24-hour numbers first.
Remove the hour of the break, then test your numbers.

vars.name: h
vars.label: hour h of the arrival time h:30 (0-23)

constraints.fail: Use a whole hour, such as 10.
The library is open from 9:00 to 18:00, so h:30 must be in that range.

steps.explain: Open times are 9:30 to 11:30 and 13:30 to 17:30 as h:30 arrivals. 12:30 is in the break, and 8:30 and 18:30 are outside the opening hours.

because.prompt: Write one or two English sentences to a friend who says 'it is open from 9 to 6, any time is fine': which times fail, and why?
hints: Which line of the sign did your friend skip?
Name the hours that fail.

checks.label: mentions the break (12, noon, lunch, midday, 낮)

selfAssess: Did I name the hour that fails?
Did I say why?
Could my friend now plan a visit?

modelAnswers.text: Between 12 and 1 it rests (쉬어요), and before 9 or after 6 it is closed.
Do not come at lunch time, 12 to 1. The library has a break then, so choose another time between 9 and 6.

badAnswers.why: Repeats the friend's mistake.
True but not about Wednesday.

because.humanReview: Whether the explanation is clear; other correct limits are accepted.

rubric.full: Picks lines 2 and 3 and rejects the name and Sunday
rubric.none: Picks the name or the Sunday line

rubric.full: Three different times that satisfy both limits
rubric.none: Times in the break or outside hours

alternatives: Arriving at 9:00 or 13:00 sharp would also be fine, but the task uses h:30 to avoid doubts at the edges.
A learner may enter 17 (17:30) and also check that the library closes at 18:00.
hardCases: '~' shows the range, but a learner may wonder whether 6시 is included; the task avoids this by using h:30.

cautions.language: 쉬어요 is glossed as 'rests'; the sign uses polite -어요 for a notice. 낮 (midday) is glossed because it is rare at K1.
cautions.culture: Korean libraries and small shops often close for lunch; 'Sunday rest' is common for smaller libraries.
cautions.accessibility: No images. A screen reader reads '~' as 'tilde' or 'to'; the material explains that it is read 'to'. The sign is given one line per row.

Each time against the constraints
Break and closed words in the explanation

subject: korean
title: Where does 'shoes off' belong?
goal: Match one sign to the place where it most likely hangs, using details of each scene, and notice what the sign leaves unsaid.
thinking: Using scene details as evidence for a match
Comparing which match fits best
Noticing what a sign does not say
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what 벗고 means. Here three scenes each contain small clues, and you must decide where the sign most likely hangs and what it still leaves open.
prerequisites: Can read short Hangul sentences
Knows that signs speak to people who enter
material:
A sign says: 신발을 벗고 들어오세요.

Words: 신발 = shoes; 벗다 = to take off; 들어오세요 = please come in.

Three places, described in words:
Place 1: a shoe shop. Customers try shoes on and walk on a thin carpet.
Place 2: a small restaurant. The dining area is a raised wooden floor with low tables. At the door a row of shoes lies on the stone step.
Place 3: a school gym. The wooden floor was polished yesterday. Students wear clean indoor shoes there.

steps.prompt: Which place fits this sign best?
hints: For each place, ask: do people there walk on the floor in their shoes?
Compare the details of the floor and of what people wear on their feet in each place.

options.reveals: You noticed that customers need their shoes on or off to try pairs; compare with the 'thin carpet' clue.
You used the raised floor and the shoes on the step as clues.
The polished floor is a reason to protect it, but students there already wear clean indoor shoes, so a 'shoes off' sign is less needed.

steps.explain: The restaurant has the clearest clues (raised floor, shoes at the step). The gym is a weaker fit because students already wear clean indoor shoes, and the shoe shop is the least likely because customers try shoes on.

steps.prompt: The sign says only: 신발을 벗고 들어오세요. Which of these questions does the sign NOT answer? Choose all.
hints: Read the sign again and mark what it tells you to do.
Then check each question against those instructions.

options.text: Where should I put my shoes?
options.reveals: You saw that the sign says to take them off, but not where to leave them.

options.text: Do I go in after taking them off?
options.reveals: 들어오세요 answers this; the sign tells you to come in.

options.text: Do I have to wear socks?
options.reveals: You noticed that the sign says nothing about socks.

options.text: Should I take my shoes off?
options.reveals: 벗고 answers this question directly.

steps.explain: The sign answers 'take shoes off' (벗고) and 'come in' (들어오세요). It does not say where to put the shoes or whether socks are needed.

rubric.full: Matches with a specific clue from the scene
rubric.none: Matches at random or by length

rubric.criterion: Sees what the sign leaves open
rubric.full: Names at least two questions it does not answer

alternatives: A learner may say the gym is also possible; the explanation shows why the restaurant is the best fit.
A learner may also say that the shoe shop is possible for a trial area; the explanation notes that it is the least likely.
hardCases: Gym floors differ between schools; the question is about the clues in this description, not general truth.

cautions.language: The sign uses -고 (and then) and the polite request -(으)세요; both are glossed by translation, not taught.
cautions.culture: Taking shoes off at the entrance is normal in Korean homes and in many traditional restaurants, but not in shoe shops.
cautions.accessibility: No images: each place is described in words. Words are given as a short glossary.

Choice of unanswered questions
human: Free-text reasons if a teacher adds a discussion

subject: korean
title: Mina checks the bakery sign
goal: Check a classmate's reasoning about a sign against the clock, find the wrong step and write the corrected step.
thinking: Checking each step of a chain of reasoning
Comparing two times
Writing the corrected reasoning
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what 열어요 means. Here the reading is correct, and the thinking is finding where the chain of reasoning breaks.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul and numbers with 시
Can compare two clock times
material:
You stand in front of a bakery at 11:00 (the clock on the wall of the shop next door says 11:00). On the bakery door is a sign:

빵집
10시에 열어요.

Words: 빵집 = bakery; 열어요 = (it) opens.

Mina read the sign and wrote her reasoning in English (below).

steps.prompt: Some of Mina's reasoning is wrong. Which is the FIRST line that is wrong?
hints: Start at line 1 and check each line in order against the sign and the clock.
Stop at the first line that does not agree with both.
lines: The sign says 열어요, so it tells when the bakery opens.
The number is 10시, so it opens at ten o'clock.
The clock says 11:00, so ten o'clock has not come yet.
So the bakery is not open, and we should wait.
steps.explain: Line 3 is wrong: 11:00 is later than 10:00, so the opening time has already passed. Line 4 repeats this error. (The sign still does not say that the door is unlocked today.)

steps.prompt: Write the correct version of line 3 in one or two English sentences.
hints: Which two times must your sentence compare?
Say which is earlier and which is later.

checks.label: mentions the time now (11 o'clock) or that the opening time has passed
says that the time has passed (after, later, already, passed)

selfAssess: Did I compare 11 and 10 correctly?
Is it clear that the opening time is already over?
Did I say something about what the bakery should be doing now?

modelAnswers.text: The clock says 11:00, which is after 10:00, so the bakery should already be open.
Ten o'clock has passed because it is eleven now, so the opening time is over.
modelAnswers.note: Says the same in other words.

modelAnswers.text: Ten o'clock has already passed, so it is open.
It is eleven now, one hour past opening.

badAnswers.text: The clock says 11:00 so we wait.
badAnswers.why: Does not mention 10 or say the time has passed.
No comparison.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sentence is clear; the cautious remark 'the sign does not say it is open today' is a good extra.

rubric.full: Picks line 3 and says why
Compares 11 and 10 and says the time has passed
rubric.partial: Gives the right conclusion without comparing

alternatives: Choosing line 4 shows seeing the wrong conclusion but not the first wrong step; the explanation names line 3 as the cause.
A learner may add that the bakery may not be open today for another reason; the sign cannot tell.
hardCases: Real bakeries sometimes open late; the sign's 10시 is the intended opening time, not a guarantee.

cautions.language: 10시 is read 'yeol-si' in native Korean numbers; the task works with the written numerals so that no spoken form is needed.
cautions.culture: Small bakeries in Korea often put opening times on the door; times use the 12-hour or 24-hour clock depending on the sign, here the plain number.
cautions.accessibility: No images; the clock is described in words. The sign is two short lines.

auto: The chosen line
Presence of 11, 10 and a 'passed' word in the correction
human: Correctness and clarity of the corrected line

subject: korean
topic: What a sign does and does not say
title: Apples are sold out. What about pears?
goal: Separate what a short sign says from what you guess, and choose the questions that would settle what the sign leaves open.
thinking: Checking each claim against the sign
Spotting a claim that goes beyond the sign
Choosing questions that settle the open point
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks what 팔았어요 means. Here the words are easy; the thinking is that a sign about apples says nothing about pears.
prerequisites: Can read short Hangul sentences
Knows the question ending -요?
material:
On the door of a fruit shop (the lights are on, a woman is arranging boxes inside) there is a sign:

사과 다 팔았어요. 내일 오세요.

Words: 사과 = apple; 배 = pear; 다 = all; 팔았어요 = sold; 내일 오세요 = please come tomorrow.

Your friend read the sign and made four notes (below). You would like to buy pears.

steps.prompt: One of your friend's notes goes beyond what the sign says. Which one?
hints: For each note, point to the word of the sign that supports it.
Which note talks about something the sign never mentions?
lines: The sign says apples are sold out.
So the shop has no apples now.
So the shop has no pears either.
The sign asks us to come back tomorrow.
steps.explain: Line 3 is the one. The sign says 사과 (apples); it says nothing about pears (배). The other lines are in the sign.

steps.prompt: You go inside to ask the woman. Which Korean questions would settle whether you can buy pears today? Choose all.
hints: Which question is about pears and about today?
Which question is about apples or about another day?

options.reveals: You asked directly about pears.
The apples are sold out, so their price does not help with the pears.
You turned the sign into a question about pears.
This is about tomorrow, not about buying pears today.

acceptable.reason: Asking 배는 있어요? alone settles the question.
Asking 배도 다 팔았어요? alone settles the question.

steps.explain: Both 배는 있어요? and 배도 다 팔았어요? ask about pears now. The questions about apple prices or tomorrow's opening time do not settle it.

rubric.full: Picks the pear line and says the sign only mentions apples
rubric.none: Picks a line the sign supports

rubric.full: Chooses both pear questions or one with a reason
rubric.partial: Chooses one pear question and one other

alternatives: Each of the two pear questions alone settles the matter.
Asking when the shop opens tomorrow is polite but does not settle today's question.
hardCases: In real shops 사과 다 팔았어요 may be an old sign that was not taken down; the task only asks what the sign says.

cautions.language: 배 is also the word for 'belly' and 'boat'; the glossary and the fruit context make the meaning clear. 팔았어요 is the past tense of 팔다 and is given in the glossary.
cautions.culture: Small fruit shops in Korea often handwrite sold-out notices on the door or on a board.
cautions.accessibility: No images; the shop is described in words. The sign is a single line of text.

auto: The chosen line
The chosen questions against the key and the acceptable sets
human: Discussion of whether an old sign can be trusted
